subtitle: Answer "are you OK?" honestly, and write down what went wrong when you're not.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 17. By the end you should be able to explain what a health check is for, why it answers 503 when the database is down, and how logger.exception records the details.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
In production nobody watches the app. Other programs visit `/health/` every few seconds and ask "are you OK?". A **load balancer** stops sending visitors to a copy that says no.

Like a nurse checking a pulse, asking isn't enough: you have to **measure**. And when it fails, write the details into the **log**, not the answer.
slides.notes: This project's /health/ view always answers ok, even when the database is down, which makes it useless. Yours will really run a tiny query. Uptime monitors and deployment tools call health checks too.

slides.title: What your code receives and returns
slides.caption: The tests build a fake `GET /health/` request and call your view directly.
slides.notes: To fake an outage, the tests swap the connection in your file for a broken one. Its error message is 'could not connect to server: password=hunter2'. Test 5 checks hunter2 is not in your response.

slides.title: New words

terms.meaning: An address other programs call to ask "is this server working?".
Shares incoming visitors between several copies of your server.
Something your app needs to work, like the database.
The object you write log lines with: `logger.error("...")`.
The "Traceback (most recent call last)" report of where an error happened.

slides.notes: An exception is Python's word for an error that happens while code runs, like ValueError. The log is the app's diary.

slides.title: Why 503, and not 200 or 500?
bullets: `2xx` success, `4xx` the client's fault, `5xx` the server's problem
**200** would be a lie: visitors keep going to a broken server
**500** usually means "my code crashed": a bug
**503** means "I'm alive, but a dependency is down. Try elsewhere."
Load balancers read the **number**, not the text

slides.title: Tools: a cursor, and the DatabaseError family
slides.caption: `SELECT` a tiny sum to prove the database answers; `DatabaseError` catches all database errors.
slides.code:
from django.db import DatabaseError, OperationalError, connection

with connection.cursor() as cursor:
    cursor.execute("SELECT 2 + 3")
    print(cursor.fetchone())

print(issubclass(OperationalError, DatabaseError))   # part of the family
slides.notes: with ... as cursor closes the cursor when the block ends. The tests raise OperationalError, a member of the DatabaseError family, so except DatabaseError catches it.

slides.title: Tool: loggers and levels
slides.caption: Without extra setup, only `WARNING` and more serious lines are shown.
slides.code:
import logging

log = logging.getLogger("shop")
log.info("A customer opened the shop")   # not shown: below WARNING
log.warning("Only 2 cups of tea left")
log.error("The till is broken")
slides.output:
Only 2 cups of tea left
The till is broken
slides.notes: Your file already has logger = logging.getLogger(__name__). In views.py that name is "views", and the tests listen to exactly that logger.

slides.title: Tool: logger.exception = message + traceback
slides.output:
Could not read the price
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<selection>", line 5, in <module>
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ten'
the program keeps going
slides.notes: Use it inside except: it logs an ERROR line and the traceback, then the program carries on. log is the shop logger from the last slide. Because the program carries on, you can still return a response after logging.

slides.title: logger.error vs logger.exception

left.heading: logger.error("...")
bullets: Writes an `ERROR` line
Only your message, **no traceback**
Works anywhere
Test 4 fails: nothing shows where it broke

right.heading: logger.exception("...")
bullets: Writes an `ERROR` line
Adds the **traceback** automatically
Use it only inside `except`
What tests 3 and 4 look for

slides.notes: At 3 a.m. the traceback is often the only clue you have. And never copy str(error) into the response instead: it can contain a password.

slides.title: Tools: JsonResponse and @require_POST
slides.notes: You'll use its sister @require_GET, already imported. Without status= a JsonResponse is 200. The Console also shows 'Method Not Allowed (GET): /ping/': that's Django logging the refused request.

slides.title: Pattern: try, log, answer safely (steps 2-4)
slides.output:
Stock check failed
Traceback (most recent call last): ...
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'lots'
{'status': 'error'}
slides.notes: Same shape as your health view, on different data. The traceback is shortened here. Risky work in try, log and give a short, safe answer in except, carry on normally otherwise. The public answer never contains the error message.

steps.text: Put `@require_GET` on the line directly above `def health(request):`
In `try:` open `with connection.cursor() as cursor:` and run `SELECT 1`
`except DatabaseError:` call `logger.exception(...)` with your own message
Then return the error dict, written by hand, with `status=503`
After the `try`/`except`, return the ok dict (status 200)

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Answering ok without a query: test 2 notices
`connection.cursor()` outside the `try`: the error escapes
Importing `connection` again inside the function: the fake is skipped
`logger.error` instead of `logger.exception`: no traceback
`str(error)` in the response: it leaks `password=hunter2`

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: You run three copies of your app behind a load balancer. One loses its database connection at 3 a.m. Its `/health/` answers 503, visitors move to the other two, and in the morning the log's traceback tells you why.
bullets: Kubernetes, Render, Railway and AWS all let you set a health check URL
They act on the **status code**, so it has to be right
Logs are how you fix problems you can't reproduce on your laptop

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: Why is a health check that always says ok useless?
Why answer 503 rather than 200 or 500 when the database is down?
Why must the error message stay out of the response?
